title: AWS Open-Sources Dogwood, Extending Cedar to Govern Sequences of Agent Tool Calls
gist: AWS open-sourced Dogwood under Apache 2.0, a policy language that extends Cedar with temporal conditions so authorization rules can read an agent's event history and constrain sequences of tool calls rather than single actions. The tradeoff is explicit: temporal conditions forfeit Cedar's automated formal reasoning and require a trusted, tenant-isolated event log — and AWS says the reference interpreter is not for production authorization.

insights.claim: AWS AgentCore Policy places authorization in a deterministic control layer outside the model: the model proposes a tool call, the policy engine accepts or rejects it, and the model never touches enforcement.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The emerging enterprise answer to agent safety is deterministic gating, not model alignment — capital and product attention should follow the control plane, not prompt-level guardrails.
insights.quote: It sits outside the model as a deterministic control layer.
insights.locator: AgentCore Policy launched at re:Invent last year

insights.claim: AWS open-sourced Dogwood under Apache 2.0 as a policy language for agent tool calls whose rules can look backward at what the agent already did, and AgentCore Policy supports it today.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: AWS is trying to set the standard for agent authorization the way it did with Cedar — open language, proprietary managed service underneath.

insights.claim: AWS contributed Cedar to the CNCF as a sandbox project in late 2025, the same open-standard playbook it is now repeating with Dogwood.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Neutral-foundation governance is AWS's adoption lever for authorization languages; watch whether Dogwood follows Cedar into the CNCF.
insights.locator: AWS contributed it to the CNCF as a sandbox project

themes.theme: Why single-request policy fails for agents

insights.claim: Cedar evaluates one request at a time and returns the same answer regardless of prior history or policy ordering, which is what makes audit and automated reasoning possible but also means it can fence off a single action and nothing more.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Statelessness is the source of both Cedar's provability and its inadequacy for agents — the tradeoff every agent-authorization vendor must now confront.
insights.quote: Feed it the same request twice, and you get the same answer, regardless of what happened before or the order the policies ran in.
insights.locator: Cedar looks at one request at a time

insights.claim: The constraints enterprises actually want on agents live in the sequence of actions — get approval before acting, stay under a running total, stop contacting external parties after touching confidential data — none of which a per-request policy language can express.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: This defines the real requirements list for agent governance products; tools that only do per-call allow/deny will not satisfy compliance buyers.
insights.quote: get approval before acting, stay under a running total, stop contacting external parties after touching confidential data

insights.claim: Dogwood adds a second clause type — a temporal condition in a 'when temporal' block alongside Cedar's 'when' — that reads the agent's event history, where events correspond to tool call requests and their outcomes carrying input arguments and requesting principal.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A minimal-surface-area extension design: the smaller the delta from Cedar, the easier enterprise adoption and tooling reuse.
insights.locator: Dogwood adds a second clause type

insights.claim: Dogwood derives its action schema directly from the agent's MCP tool manifest, one action per tool, generating the policy surface automatically rather than requiring hand-authored action definitions.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: MCP is becoming the de facto schema substrate that downstream governance tooling generates from — a durable standardization signal.
insights.locator: The action schema comes from the agent's MCP tool manifest

insights.claim: Under the hood Dogwood translates a temporal condition into a Cedar context field that its interpreter populates from event history before Cedar makes the decision, preserving Cedar as the underlying decision engine.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The implementation is a preprocessing layer, not a new engine — meaning existing Cedar deployments and tooling can absorb it cheaply.
insights.locator: Under the hood, a temporal condition is translated

insights.claim: Dogwood exposes four temporal operators — formerly, count_within, count_distinct_within and sum_within — plus a bind operator to name an aggregate, all defined as standard-library macros over a core Metric First-Order Temporal Logic subset rather than as language primitives.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Macro-over-a-formal-core design keeps the trusted computing base small and extensible — a sign the language is built to add operators without re-verifying the kernel.
insights.locator: Four operators cover the common shapes

insights.claim: Every valid Cedar policy is also a valid Dogwood policy, deny-by-default is retained and forbid still overrides permit, so existing Cedar policy sets migrate without rewriting.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Zero-rewrite compatibility removes the main adoption barrier for existing Cedar users — a deliberate lock-in-friendly upgrade path.
insights.quote: Any valid Cedar policy is also a valid Dogwood policy, so nothing needs rewriting.

insights.claim: A rate limit written against response events instead of request events can be defeated by concurrency: AWS's own trace shows three concurrent $2,000 transfers arriving before any settles, so a policy summing responses sees nothing in flight and allows all three past a $5,000 cap, while the same policy summing requests denies the third.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Spending caps on agents can be silently bypassed by a one-word policy error — a concrete, auditable failure mode for anyone underwriting agentic financial workflows.
insights.quote: One word separates the two policies.
insights.locator: The most instructive part of the announcement

insights.claim: Because agents issue parallel tool calls and multi-agent settings compound the interleaving, a policy that reads correctly in sequence can fail under concurrency — a familiar distributed systems problem arriving in authorization.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Agent governance inherits decades of distributed-systems hazards; expect an emerging market for policy testing and race-condition analysis tooling.
insights.quote: A policy that reads correctly in sequence can fail under concurrency, which is a familiar distributed systems problem arriving somewhere new.

insights.claim: Temporal conditions in Dogwood forfeit the automated reasoning analysis tools Cedar provides, so a policy set using them can no longer be formally analyzed — which AWS states is precisely why it built a separate language rather than extending Cedar.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Formal verifiability and sequence-awareness are currently mutually exclusive in agent authorization; regulated buyers must choose, and whoever closes that gap has a real moat.
insights.quote: temporal conditions do not support the automated reasoning analysis tools Cedar provides, so a policy set using them loses the ability to be formally analyzed
insights.locator: AWS is direct about the costs

insights.claim: Dogwood temporal evaluation requires stateful event tracking and its evaluation time can depend on the length of the event log, introducing a latency profile that scales with agent history.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Authorization latency now grows with agent session length — a real operational cost that favors managed services with optimized event stores.
insights.locator: Temporal evaluation requires stateful tracking of events

insights.claim: The Apache 2.0 license does not make Dogwood deployable: AWS says the reference interpreter is for exploring and testing the language, not for running authorization in production.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing the spec while withholding a production implementation steers real deployments to AWS's managed AgentCore Policy — read the release as standard-setting, not commoditization.
insights.quote: The Apache 2.0 license is not an invitation to deploy.
insights.locator: The Apache 2.0 license is not an invitation to deploy

insights.claim: Running Dogwood safely requires trusted timestamps, authenticated events, consistent field and action names, durable trace storage, decision logging, strict cross-tenant isolation of histories and a retention policy for sensitive tool-call data — effectively building a trustworthy event log before any policy has meaning.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The real cost of agent governance is the audited event-log infrastructure, not the policy language — that is where budget and third-party vendors will land.
insights.quote: It amounts to building an event log you can trust. Without that, the policies mean nothing.
insights.locator: The repository is blunt about the rest

insights.claim: Dogwood landed in the same week the MCP 2026-07-28 specification made agent traffic legible to HTTP infrastructure via required method and tool-name headers, with headers letting a gateway see which tool an agent is calling and Dogwood expressing what a sequence of those calls may add up to.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The observability and enforcement halves of agent governance are standardizing simultaneously — 2026 is the year agent traffic becomes controllable by existing network infrastructure.
insights.quote: The two solve adjacent halves of one problem.
insights.locator: The release lands in the same week the MCP 2026-07-28 specification

insights.claim: Dogwood's roadmap includes absolute-time windows anchored to wall-clock boundaries, liveness properties asserting what must eventually happen rather than what must not, and orchestration policies for multi-agent handoffs and locks.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Liveness and multi-agent orchestration policy signal where AWS expects enterprise agent deployments to go next — worth tracking as a leading indicator of production multi-agent adoption.

insights.claim: The Dogwood release was co-authored by Marc Brooker, an AWS VP and distinguished engineer who led the Aurora DSQL launch, with Joseph Tassarotti of the Automated Reasoning Group and Jean-Baptiste Tristan of AWS Agentic AI, and AWS is not yet accepting external contributions pending feedback and language stabilization.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Senior distributed-systems and formal-methods talent assigned to agent authorization signals AWS treats this as strategic infrastructure, not a side project.
insights.locator: Marc Brooker, a VP and distinguished engineer at AWS
